subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Writing: Spelling (Double Consonants)
overview: Some words need a consonant written twice. In this sub-strand you will spell words such as collect, borrow, bill, loss and offer, and you will double a consonant when you add -ing or -ed to short verbs such as shop. Correct double letters keep your writing about money clear.

lessons.title: Seeing and spelling double consonants
objectives: Spell common words that contain double consonants.
Double the final consonant of a short verb before -ing or -ed.
Hear that the double letter is still one sound.
lessons.intro: Say collect. You hear one l, but the spelling needs two. Leave one out and the word looks unfinished. Money words are full of these quiet doubles.
lessons.notes:
### Words that already have a double letter
Say the word, then spell the pair aloud so you do not drop a letter.

- collect: co-ll-ect. We collect fees or coins.
- borrow: bo-rr-ow. If you borrow money, you must pay it back.
- bill: bi-ll. A bill is a note of what must be paid.
- till: ti-ll. A till holds money during a sale.
- loss: lo-ss. A loss means you got back less than you spent.
- offer: o-ff-er. To offer is to say what you are willing to pay or to give.
- sell: se-ll. To sell is to give goods for money.
- success: su-cc-e-ss. Success has both cc and ss.
- account: a-cc-ount. An account can mean a record of money, including money kept at a bank.
- letter, little, happy, class, address: le-tt-er, li-tt-le, ha-pp-y, cla-ss, a-dd-re-ss.

The double letters make one sound. You write two because that is the spelling, not because you say the sound twice.

### Doubling before -ing and -ed
Some short verbs end with one vowel and one consonant: shop, stop, plan, drop. When you add -ing or -ed, double the last consonant.

- shop → shopping, shopped
- stop → stopping, stopped
- plan → planning, planned
- drop → dropping, dropped

Do not double when the verb already ends with two consonants: help → helping, collect → collecting. Do not add a third l to collect.

Do not double when the vowel is made by two letters, as in clean → cleaning, or when the verb ends in w, x or y: play → playing, mix → mixing.

A quick test: if the verb is short, has one vowel letter, and ends with one consonant, double that consonant before -ing or -ed.

### From a dictation
'Please collect the bills. Do not borrow from the till. A loss must be written in the account. We stopped shopping when the list was finished.'

Every doubled consonant in that dictation is doing spelling work. Missing one changes the look of the word and can slow the reader.

keyWords.meaning: the same consonant written twice in a row, such as ll, ss or rr
a written note of money that must be paid
a record of money received and spent, or money kept at a bank
one of the letters a, e, i, o, u

examples.problem: How do you spell the -ing form of shop?
steps: Shop has one vowel, o, and one final consonant, p.

examples.problem: Which spelling is correct: colect, collet or collect?
steps: The word has a double l after co.

activity.title: Dictation and jigsaw words
steps: Listen to the dictation in the notes and write it. Underline every double consonant.
Use letter cards like a jigsaw to build collect, borrow, bill, loss and offer.
Add -ing to shop, stop, plan and help. Decide which three need a double consonant.
Check with a partner and correct any missing letter at once.

practice.question: Spell these words: collect, borrow, loss, offer.
Write the -ing form of plan and of clean.
Why do we write two l letters in bill if we say only one sound?
practice.answer: Because the correct spelling uses ll, even though the sound is single.

summary: Learn the double letters in collect, borrow, bill, loss, offer and success.
Double the final consonant of a short verb such as shop before -ing or -ed.
Do not double a verb that already ends with two consonants.

lessons.title: Sentences with double consonants
objectives: Unjumble letters to make words with double consonants.
Use those words in correct sentences.
Explain why clear spelling matters in writing about money.
lessons.intro: A jumbled word is a puzzle. A bill with a missing letter is a problem, because the reader may stop and wonder what you meant. The same spelling skill serves both the game and the real writing.
lessons.notes:
### Unjumble, then check the pairs
Each answer must contain the double consonant. Count the letters before you decide you have finished.

- tcelloc → collect (7 letters, ll)
- worrbo → borrow (6 letters, rr)
- llbi → bill (4 letters, ll)
- ssol → loss (4 letters, ss)
- ffero → offer (5 letters, ff)
- ccusses → success (7 letters, cc and ss)

If your word is one letter short, the missing letter is often the second one of a pair.

### Sentences that stay true
Correct spelling should carry a true meaning.

- We collect the school fees every Monday and write them in the book.
- Do not borrow money you cannot pay back.
- The bill was clear, so we paid it.
- A loss is not the same as a profit.
- The seller will offer a fair price.
- They stopped shopping when the money in the tin was finished.
- Please sell the extra seedlings and record the amount.

Notice stopped and shopping. Both come from short verbs, so the consonant is doubled.

### Why the letters matter
Writing is communication. If bill becomes bil, or loss becomes lose, the reader has to guess. Lose is a different word: it means not to win, or to be unable to find something. Loss is the noun for the money result. One letter changes the word.

In a list of fees, a record of a debt, or a note about a profit, clear spelling lets the next reader trust the writing. Check double letters before you hand work in. Spell the pair in your head: two l's, two r's, two s's. That small pause prevents a muddy sentence.

Honest, careful writing about money is part of being understood. The letters are not decoration. They are the word.

keyWords.meaning: to put mixed-up letters into the correct word
to write information down so it can be checked later
a naming word, such as loss or bill

examples.problem: Unjumble worrbo and use it in a sentence about money.
steps: The letters make borrow, with rr.
The sentence should show that borrowed money is paid back.
examples.answer: borrow. Example: If you borrow a coin, pay it back.

examples.problem: Choose loss or lose: The business made a ______ . Do not ______ the receipt.
steps: Loss is the noun for the money result.
examples.answer: The business made a loss. Do not lose the receipt.

activity.title: Peer dictation of sentences
steps: Build three words from jumbled letters with a partner, then say the double consonant aloud.
Each learner dictates three sentences that use words with double consonants. The partner writes them.
Mark the doubles together. Correct any word that has lost a letter.
Write two new sentences about saving or paying a fee, and underline the double consonants.

practice.question: Write a sentence using offer and bill.
practice.answer: Example: The seller will offer a lower price if the bill is paid today.

practice.question: Correct: We stoped shoping when the money was finished.
practice.answer: We stopped shopping when the money was finished.

practice.question: Why does spelling loss with ss matter?
practice.answer: Loss is the noun. A missing s makes the word look like lose, which is a different word, so the reader may be confused.

summary: Unjumble carefully and count the letters in each pair.
Use the words in true sentences about money.
Clear double consonants help the reader trust what you wrote.

quiz.question: Which word has a double r?
quiz.explanation: Borrow has rr. Bill has ll, loss has ss, offer has ff.

quiz.question: Which word doubles both c and s?
The -ing form of shop is
quiz.explanation: Double the p, then add ing. Do not add a third p.

quiz.question: The -ed form of stop is
quiz.explanation: Stop doubles the p before ed.

quiz.question: Which sentence is spelled correctly?
quiz.explanation: Collect has ll and a single c at the start and before t.

quiz.question: Choose the correct pair: The shop made a ______. Do not ______ the bill.
quiz.explanation: Loss is the noun. Lose is the verb meaning to misplace something or fail to keep it.

quiz.question: Why do we double the p in shopping?
quiz.answer: Shop is a short verb with one vowel and one final consonant, so the p is doubled before -ing.
quiz.explanation: That is the doubling rule for verbs such as shop, stop and plan.

quiz.question: Why is correct spelling important when you write about money?
quiz.answer: The reader can trust words such as bill, loss and collect and does not have to guess a different word.
quiz.explanation: Clear spelling is part of clear written communication.
